WalkthroughText: A void method performs an action but hands back no value, so you call it as its own statement — just its name and parentheses followed by a semicolon, never assigned to a variable. When the call executes, Java pauses the current method, pushes a brand-new stack frame for the called method with its own parameters, runs that method's statements line by line, and then pops the frame off the stack once it finishes, returning control to the exact line right after the call in the caller. Watching the stack frame appear and disappear, alongside the highlighted line jumping between caller and callee, is the key to understanding how void calls actually work under the hood.

Choices: Compile error because printLine has no return statement
PracticeItems.Explanation: Calling printLine("Hello") pushes a new frame that runs its body, printing "Line: Hello", and then that frame is popped and control returns to main, which then prints "Done". A void method never needs a return statement, so there is no compile error, and both lines are printed in order.

Choices: It compiles and prints "Hi there" then 0
It compiles and prints "Hi there" then some garbage value
It fails to compile because greet() returns void and cannot be assigned to an int
It fails to compile because greet() is missing parameters
PracticeItems.Explanation: greet() is declared void, meaning the call produces no value at all. Trying to store the result of a void call in a variable (int x = greet();) is a compile-time error, not a runtime issue, so nothing ever prints.

Choices: Twice; Count is 3 then Count is 5
Twice; Count is 3 then Count is 3
PracticeItems.Explanation: Each call to showCount(a) and showCount(a + 2) pushes its own separate frame with its own copy of parameter n (3, then 5), runs to completion, prints its line, and pops back to main before the next call happens. So control leaves main twice, printing 'Count is 3' then 'Count is 5'.

WalkthroughSteps.Caption: We start with a main method about to call a void method named printMessage. Right now only main's frame exists on the stack.
Main reaches the statement printMessage("hi"); this is a call to a void method, so it's written as a stand-alone statement, not assigned to anything.
Java pauses main right here and pushes a brand-new stack frame for printMessage, since a method call always creates its own frame.
The argument "hi" is copied into printMessage's own parameter variable named text, living only inside this new frame.
Execution now highlights the first line inside printMessage's body — control has fully moved into the callee's frame.
printMessage runs its System.out.println statement, printing 'Message: hi' to the console, using its local text variable.
printMessage has no more statements and no return value to send back, so its frame is popped right off the stack.
Control returns to main at the exact line right after the call, and main's frame is still exactly as it was before the call.
Main continues executing its next statement, showing that calling a void method simply pauses the caller, runs the callee to completion, then resumes right where it left off.
